items.item: earlier schemes including Gorilla and Chimp128 have compression ratios not better than general-purpose compressors such as Zstd, while decompression is much slower

items.item: ALP losslessly encodes doubles as integers if they originated as decimals, and otherwise compresses the doubles' front bits in vectors designed to auto-vectorise

items.item: The ALP algorithm is the default compression method for floating-point numbers in DuckDB

items.item: A 12x reduction isn't a property of the Gorilla algorithm in the abstract — it's a property of the algorithm applied to data with a specific shape (regular timestamps, slowly changing values), so quoting the number without the data that produced it promises something the algorithm alone can't keep.

at.step: Hook: the same algorithm, a very different ratio

items.item: Reproducing the paper's own worked bit counts exactly, rather than trusting its prose description of the rule, is what turns 'the algorithm does X' into a checked claim instead of a restated one.

at.step: Reveal: delta-of-delta timestamps and XOR'd floats

items.item: The honest answer to 'does the same encoder give the same ratio on different data' is not a single number — it's that the ratio is a function of two inputs, the encoder and the data, and changing either one changes the output.

at.step: Predict: same encoder, same ratio on a different signal?

items.item: A noisy float with many significant digits defeats delta-of-delta and XOR encoding for the same underlying reason: both rely on successive values being close to each other, and noise by definition isn't.

at.step: Reveal: three regimes, three very different ratios

items.item: A refinement that only wins under a specific further condition (here, a repeating pattern a wider match window can find) is not a strictly better algorithm — it's a different bet about what the data looks like, and the bet can lose on data the original algorithm wins on.

at.step: Reveal: Chimp's threshold, and the wider window that helps

items.item: ALP's advantage isn't that it compresses harder than Gorilla in general — it's that it targets a specific, common failure mode (decimal values whose low bits are measurement noise, not information) that bit-pattern codecs can't see because they operate on the float's raw bits, not its decimal meaning.

at.step: Reveal: ALP's decimal-aware encoding, and why it wins here

items.item: A tag column repeating the same few strings millions of times and a value column that changes every reading are different compression problems with different right answers — applying a value-shaped codec to a label-shaped column, or vice versa, wastes the properties each data type actually has.

at.step: Reveal: dictionary and RLE shrink the tags, not the values

items.item: A lossy codec that drops points within an error band is solving a different problem than a lossless codec that keeps every bit — stating the error bound explicitly is what keeps 'we compressed it more' from quietly becoming 'we changed what the data says.'

at.step: Recap

items.item: The real lesson of the Facebook-to-plant gap isn't that Gorilla is overrated — it's that a compression ratio quoted without its data's shape is a promise with a hidden precondition, and the fix is to measure your own data's shape, not to distrust the published number.

at.step: Recap

items.item: A measurement that only reports the best-case regime for each codec would make every codec look interchangeable; reporting bytes per point across all three regimes for every codec is what actually lets a reader pick the right tool for their own data instead of the tool with the best marketing number.
